extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of political and theological philosophy (seventeenth-century and modern readers of Hobbes), clergy, sovereigns, and scholars of Christian doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of what articles of Christian faith are necessary for salvation, how faith is produced and mediated, the relation of faith to obedience and civil authority, and causes/errors of spiritual darkness. The text gives normative claims about doctrine, authority, and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith comes by hearing (mediation by lawful teachers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary immediate cause of belief in Christian doctrine is hearing the Scripture taught by lawful pastors, parents, and appointed teachers (cf. Rom. 10:17).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faith is normally produced by instruction from authorized teachers; differences in commonwealths' teaching explain differences in public belief. Anti-pattern: treating 'why we believe' as purely epistemic 'how we know' and ignoring the social/teaching means. Example passages: Paul’s questions about hearing and preachers, and observations that Christians are taught from infancy in Christian commonwealths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith is ultimately a gift of God
rubrics_metrics.description: Although instruction by teachers is the ordinary means, faith itself is a gift from God given to whom He wills; therefore the presence of teaching does not imply that faith is purely human achievement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: in a school the master causes learning for some but learning is ultimately a good thing that comes from God; claimants to immediate inspiration (prophets) are subject to church examination. Scoring note: do not conflate the causal role of teaching with the metaphysical origin of faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only strictly necessary article of faith for salvation: 'Jesus is the Christ'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Scripture makes simply necessary to salvation the belief that Jesus is the Christ (the promised King/Messiah).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple arguments offered: scope of the evangelists (the Gospels aim to establish this article), sermons of the apostles, the easiness of the doctrine (examples like the thief on the cross), clear/plain scriptural texts (John 20:31; John 11:26; 1 John), and the foundation-role of the article (Matthew 16:18; 1 Cor. 3). Anti-pattern: demanding assent to disputed secondary doctrines (e.g., transubstantiation, purgatory) as necessary for salvation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief that Jesus is the Christ is sufficient for baptism and entry into the kingdom of God
rubrics_metrics.description: Confessions of faith that directly or by consequence imply that Jesus is the Christ are presented in Scripture as grounds for baptism and salvation (e.g., Acts 8:36-37; John passages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Eunuch's confession before baptism, the thief's simple plea on the cross. Interpretation: where Scripture says 'thy faith hath saved thee' it often refers to such confessions. Anti-pattern: elevating more complex doctrinal formulations as prerequisites for baptism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other doctrinal articles are implicit or deducible from the foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: Other beliefs (God's omnipotence, Christ's resurrection, general resurrection) are either contained in or deducible from the foundational belief that Jesus is the Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A man who truly holds that Jesus is the Son and Messiah thereby holds, explicitly or implicitly, the consequences that follow; therefore requiring separate assent to each is unnecessary. Practical implication: simple faith in the foundation can encompass more complex theology even if the believer cannot articulate all deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith and obedience (repentance) together necessary for salvation
rubrics_metrics.description: Both an inward assent (faith) and the will to obey God (repentance/obedience) are jointly required for salvation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural support: Acts 2 (Peter's call to 'Repent, and be baptized'); Mark 1:15 ('Repent and believe the Gospel'); Luke 18 (the good ruler told to sell all and follow Christ). Operationally, faith supplies the plea that God accepts; obedience supplies the will that God accepts as indicative of repentance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different senses of justification: how faith and works contribute
rubrics_metrics.description: Justification can mean (1) being declared just by the will/endeavour to obey (the will accepted), or (2) being acquitted when one’s plea is accepted despite insufficiency; in the latter sense faith makes the plea effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between 'justice' as disposition/will (which God may accept) and legal discharge of the law. Anti-pattern: conflating 'justified by works' with complete legal satisfaction of the law; instead accept the nuanced combined role of faith and will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience to the civil sovereign is not inconsistent with obedience to God
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects may lawfully obey their civil sovereign (Christian or infidel) because civil laws include laws of nature and parts of church law; the sovereign represents the church in making laws within the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the sovereign is Christian, his commands are generally to be obeyed; if he draws false consequences, he may err but still be saved; when sovereign forbids some profession of opinion, private individuals lack ground to disobey without church appointment to judge. Practical rule: civil obedience stands unless legitimately judged otherwise by proper church authority. Anti-pattern: private resistance or judgment over sovereign matters when the matter concerns obedience rather than doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct under an infidel sovereign: internal faith permitted, public disobedience not generally required
rubrics_metrics.description: When the sovereign is an infidel, Christians are to keep their internal faith and may expect heavenly reward for suffering rather than provoke rebellion; resistance is typically sinful unless there is a just cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to Naaman: internal religion is permissible; martyrs who voluntarily accept persecution may receive reward but should not necessarily expect to cause civil resistance. Anti-pattern: using private faith as license for public disobedience or rebellion against lawful sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret Scripture by scope and main design, not isolated texts
rubrics_metrics.description: True interpretation of Scripture depends on the scope and principal design of the writer; isolated proof-texting without regard to the whole makes texts obscure and leads to error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: consider the plain sense, harmony, and scope of Scripture; avoid 'casting atoms of Scripture' (isolated verses) to obscure doctrine. Anti-pattern: insisting on single texts out of context to support contentious positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and nature of the Kingdom of Darkness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Kingdom of Darkness is a confederacy of deceivers (Satan, phantasms, daemons) who, by dark and erroneous doctrines, extinguish the light of nature and Gospel in people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an allegorical description: 'children of darkness' are those under the dominion of false doctrines and phantasms. Practical implication: beware doctrines which derive from phantasms or fabricated traditions rather than Scripture’s plain sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main causes of spiritual darkness/misinterpretation of Scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: Four principal causes: (1) abusing and misinterpreting Scripture; (2) introducing heathen 'daemonology' and fabulous accounts (ghosts, fairies); (3) mixing in Greek vain philosophy (especially Aristotle); (4) mingling false or uncertain traditions and invented history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each of these corrupts understanding: misuse of Scripture leads to doctrinal error; pagan fables create phantasms; imported philosophy obscures revelation; uncertain traditions perpetuate error. Anti-pattern: giving heed to seducing spirits or to those who 'speak lies in hypocrisy' and rely on conscience seared against truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error of identifying the present Church with the Kingdom of God
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistaking the present visible Church for the political Kingdom of God leads to claims of universal ecclesiastical authority (one man or assembly speaking for Christ) and to political and religious confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include claims of papal vicarship, the necessity of episcopal coronation for kings, excommunications absolving subjects of obedience, and the division of clergy/laity with claims to divine revenue. Anti-pattern: treating ecclesiastical institutions as identical with the theocratic polity instituted under Moses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of papal claims and their political consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The papal claim to be Christ’s vicar on earth and to possess regal powers (e.g., authority to absolve subjects from obedience) is presented as a doctrinal-political error that produces civil discord and mistaking of loyalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Lateran Council clause regarding kings purging heresy and subjects being absolved if king fails — used to create political instability. Practical warning: ecclesiastical jurisdiction should not be conflated with civil sovereignty; such conflation breeds misdirected obedience and conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins and problems of the clergy/laity distinction and ecclesiastical revenues
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between clergy and laity and the appropriation of tithes arose from mistaking the Christian Church for Israel’s theocratic arrangement (Levitical inheritance), leading to double tribute and excessive clerical revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical explanation: clergy claimed maintenance analogous to Levites because they treated the Church as God’s political inheritance; consequence: burdens on people and confusion of civil and divine claims. Anti-pattern: accepting clerical exactions as jure divino without scrutiny of their historical-biblical basis.
